extracted.intended_audience: Reuters journalists, bureau chiefs, specialist editors and newsroom managers
extracted.subtask_description: Company editorial handbook guidance on legal risks and newsroom procedures for Reuters journalists and editors, covering incident reporting, defamation, contempt, copyright, privacy, data protection and where to get legal support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident report: when to file
rubrics_metrics.description: An incident report must be filed when staff are injured, killed, imperilled or harassed; Reuters is threatened with legal action as a result of a story or staff behaviour; Reuters withdraws a story/graphic/photo/video; Reuters makes a mistake that adversely affects a customer and/or prompts a large number of angry calls; Reuters is the target of a hoax or attempted hoax; serious allegations of wrongdoing are levelled against employees; service is seriously disrupted to customers; involvement in an issue that could embarrass the company; involvement in an issue/controversy that could result in an analyst's or reporter's question to a company official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list does not cover every eventuality — 'err on the side of caution' and ensure supervisors are aware of serious situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident report: how to file and update
rubrics_metrics.description: When a serious incident occurs, contact your direct supervisor by telephone or e-mail and then file an incident report using the Corporate Incident Notification Site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You or your supervisor should update your report on that site until the matter is closed. Managing editors must make sure bureau chiefs/specialist editors are aware of relevant incidents in other regions and keep a regional register; a central database will be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes and other records
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep good records of interviews, notes, etc.; if possible tape interviews (subject to local law). If you take notes, keep them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid typing notes straight into a computer and then using them without keeping the original; print, date and file initial notes as contemporaneous record — lawsuits may come months or years later and a good set of notes is invaluable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Speed is important but speed without accuracy is an invitation for trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use all sources available to check accuracy; check official sources (e.g. court registries) rather than relying on rumours or a single source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Always obtain the other side of the story and give the other side every opportunity to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't elicit a comment initially, call again and record all attempts; if they decline to comment, note that down — these notes are vital to demonstrate genuine efforts to offer opportunity to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes from third parties often land us in trouble; using a quote does not remove liability for defamatory content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a quote is potentially defamatory, think carefully about where and how you use it; make sure you can back it up, have a good record of it and offer a balancing view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnamed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Some courts consider that if you cannot reveal a source it could mean you have no source at all — suggesting fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a court demands disclosure and you refuse you may face fines or imprisonment for contempt; be aware of the legal risk of relying on unnamed sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: A healthy dose of scepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why are they telling me this?" — sources may provide information to further their own cause and it may be skewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a well‑rounded story with balance, not just one side; scrutinise source motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your work has a global reach
rubrics_metrics.description: What you write is published in many jurisdictions other than where you write; legal issues in other countries may apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, alert editors and seek legal advice because something acceptable locally may cause trouble elsewhere (especially re: defamation and contempt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention editor (ATTN EDITOR) flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the warning flag ATTN EDITOR (or ATTN ED) in any story you think may be legally dangerous or may affect the reputation of Reuters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain reasons to the editing desk in a separate coded message using the same codes as the story; the desk should refer it to the editor in charge. All reporters must understand when and how to use the flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation policy: applying English law worldwide
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters applies the principles of English defamation law worldwide because English law is generally more stringent and damages are typically higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal concepts described generally refer to English law; be aware of jurisdictional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is defamation?
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation is the statement to a third party of words or other matter containing an untrue imputation against the character of another. Libel covers publication (including TV, radio, Internet, email, blogs, chatrooms) and slander covers the spoken word.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a defamatory statement?
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, publication of a statement which 'tends to lower the claimant in the estimation of right‑thinking people.' Definitions vary by jurisdiction and over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement’s meaning (ordinary meaning, implied meaning, or innuendo) is crucial to whether it is defamatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common defamatory imputations
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil actions commonly fall into: (1) imputations of dishonourable conduct or motives; (2) disparaging a person in their job (suggestions of incompetence or substandard services); (3) statements causing a person to be shunned or implying financial difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation and images
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation is not limited to words; pictures combined with words can cause defamation, e.g. misidentification of a person in a picture as a terrorism suspect or using a stock photo that identifies an unrelated person/company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using identifiable images that have no connection to the story; misidentification has 'no excuse'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may sue for defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimant may be an individual or a company in respect of trading reputation, or any incorporated body; some jurisdictions prohibit government departments, local authorities or political parties from suing, but individuals within these organisations can if identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, check jurisdictional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a defamation action
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally the claimant must establish: (1) the words were defamatory; (2) the claimant is identified; (3) there was publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If established, the action will succeed unless the publisher can offer a defence such as truth, fair comment or privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 1 — Is it defamatory (meaning/innuendo)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court assesses whether the words defamed the claimant in ordinary meaning, implied meaning, or innuendo; innuendo depends on readers' extra knowledge (example given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many statements have more than one meaning; courts decide if the meaning is defamatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 2 — Identification of claimant
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimant must show they were identified; naming is not required — in England it is sufficient if people who know the claimant would understand the words to refer to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a group is so large no individual can claim identification, no action; if group is small enough individuals could sue — consider naming the individual rather than implying membership of a small group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 3 — Publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication includes almost all methods of communication (email, Internet, chatrooms, broadcasts); publication to a third party is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any person/company taking part in publication can be liable (writer, printer, publisher, distributor); some limited defences exist for printers/distributors/ISPs who took all reasonable care and had no reason to believe the defamation would occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: Truth/justification
rubrics_metrics.description: In England it is a complete defence that the words are substantially true; some countries require publication for the public benefit as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defendant is presumed to have published a false statement until proved otherwise; it is not necessary to prove every allegation if the unproven parts do not materially injure reputation; past allegations may not be defendable if they suggest a continuing taint on character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: Fair comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Protects statements of honestly held opinion on matters of true fact; useful when reporting comments by others (e.g. politicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defeated if comment is made maliciously (recklessly or carelessly). When facts underpinning the comment are from a privileged occasion (e.g. parliamentary or court proceedings), it may not be necessary to prove truth of allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: Absolute privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute privilege protects statements in parliamentary proceedings, judicial proceedings, state proceedings, statements by certain public officials, and reports of parliamentary/judicial proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication on privileged occasions is absolutely protected and the maker need not fear defamation claims from injured parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: Statutory qualified privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified privilege protects communications where there is a public interest in the statement being made and received, e.g. fair and accurate reports of parliamentary or judicial proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privilege is defeated by malice and will only attach if reporting is fair, accurate and contemporaneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: Common‑law qualified privilege and the Reynolds factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Common‑law qualified privilege may protect statements outside statutory protection where the publisher has a duty to publish and the public has an interest in receiving it. The leading case suggested 10 tests (the Reynolds Defence) for courts to consider when deciding whether publication should be privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 10 tests include: seriousness of allegation; public concern; source of information; steps taken to verify; status of information; urgency; whether comment was sought from complainant; whether gist of complainant's version was included; tone of article; circumstances/timing of publication. Recent developments require that the story must also satisfy a public interest test (not merely public interest curiosity). Failure to seek comment or to write a balanced piece are common reasons the defence fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt: general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Contempt of court involves interference with the administration of justice — either in a particular case or with the judicial process generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guidance focuses on contempt issues most pertinent to Reuters: court reporting restrictions and protecting sources; refer to Legal Department for comprehensive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt: court reporting restrictions and common dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Media are usually allowed in courtrooms but many jurisdictions impose restrictions to protect people involved or ensure administration of justice (e.g. not allowed to report identity of a sexual‑offence victim or minors). Some countries allow judges to impose specific restriction orders (family/domestic cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatest dangers include: assuming guilt of accused; disclosing previous convictions; publishing photographs where identity is an issue; publishing material during a trial that the jury should not be aware of. UK law can impose strict liability; internal procedures exist for cross‑jurisdictional conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt: protecting sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to disclose a source may lead to contempt of court if the court deems disclosure necessary for administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions can include incarceration and fines; escalate any issues to senior editors and the Legal Department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for handling stories that risk contempt (internet publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions on publishing material outside jurisdictions with contempt risks must be taken by the global managing editor and appropriate global specialist editor in consultation with regional equivalents, based on internal and external legal advice and assessment of probable risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the risk of prosecution (UK contempt = SERIOUS risk of SUBSTANTIAL prejudice) against news value. If published, apply an advisory note (e.g. 'This story is not for use in the United Kingdom [or other jurisdiction], where its publication may be deemed to constitute contempt of court'); do not carry on reuters.co.uk or local site in that jurisdiction; consider regional changes and transmission variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright: basic principle and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects the skill and labour that produce a literary, artistic, dramatic or musical work once it is recorded; without permission it is not permitted to use a substantial part of another's copyright work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never plagiarise; Reuters would not expect a journalist to be accused of infringing someone else's copyright if they created work independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and stringers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work is created by an employee in the scope of employment the copyright belongs to the employer; if created by a contractor (stringer) then copyright belongs to the contractor unless an agreement says otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always have a stringer sign a stringer contract (or make ownership clear in writing) to avoid disputes; contact Legal Department for the standard contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to do if others infringe Reuters copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: If you discover content infringement by third parties using Reuters articles or material without proper credit, bring it to the attention of the Media Sales team in your region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the infringing party is a non‑client it is a sales opportunity; if a client it may breach contract — escalate persistent infringement to the Legal Department via Media Sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to privacy and publication of images
rubrics_metrics.description: Many countries prohibit publication of a person's image without consent (particularly civil law jurisdictions), with exceptions for reporting current affairs when publication is in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For well‑known people, pictures may be used if they are part of current affairs and not in a place where they have an expectation of privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public and non‑public places — expectation of privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of a picture taken in a non‑public place where a person may have an expectation of privacy is likely to infringe that right; boundaries are not always clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rule of thumb: put yourself in the shoes of the subject — would you feel your privacy invaded and could publication be defended as in the public interest?

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrities — extra caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrities are more likely to bring claims for infringement and recent developments have been driven by celebrity lawsuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be extra cautious with images of celebrities, especially if origin or location (non‑public place) is questionable or telephoto lenses are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures of minors
rubrics_metrics.description: Always be sensitive when taking and publishing photographs of children; minors are often a special protected category and may be incapable of giving legally effective consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a child agrees, families/guardians could challenge publication — exercise caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of private information — newsworthiness vs gratuitous detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the detail adds to the newsworthiness of the story or is gratuitous private information not in the public interest; some jurisdictions prohibit identifying victims of certain crimes (e.g. rape).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defence is publication in the public interest — distinguish 'public interest' from 'interest to the public' (salacious gossip often fails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data protection law and journalism exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Data protection law protects processing and transfer of personal data (any information that can identify an individual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a special exemption for journalism if compliance is incompatible with journalistic purposes; the area is complex and varies by country — contact the Legal Department if in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional legal information and support (follow‑the‑sun model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Counsel's Office maintains a global follow‑the‑sun legal support model with in‑house lawyers on call and available at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First point of contact should be the identified regional lawyers; if unavailable contact lawyers in a region in its working day. Use 'Lex Editorial' email or lexeditorial@reuters.com to reach all lawyers. Regional external counsel contacts are available where in‑house lawyers are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal investments disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you report on a company in which you or your family has any kind of shareholding or other financial interest you must notify the interest to your manager or bureau chief.
